newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia poll brings little hope of political peace.
newsitem.headline: Zambia poll brings little hope of political peace.

text.p: Zambia holds elections on Monday that were meant to cement democracy but have instead embroiled the southern African country in a row over how well it adheres to democratic rules.

President Frederick Chiluba faces four challengers for his post, but his only real rival is a man who is not even standing -- his veteran predecessor, Kenneth Kaunda, a pioneer of African independence who fell from grace after mismanaging the economy.

Kaunda, now main opposition leader, and smaller parties joining a boycott of the election accuse Chiluba of breaking the pledge of democracy which won him power in 1991 and ended nearly three decades of Kaunda's socialist-oriented rule.

They say he has changed the constitution, intimidated the media and rigged the registration of voters to cling to power. "This country faces a deep-rooted crisis. Please don't vote on Monday," Kaunda told a weekend rally.

Foreign donors have frozen desperately needed aid, saying a new law passed in May, ruling out candidates whose parents were born abroad, seemed clearly aimed at 72-year-old Kaunda who is of Malawian descent.

A defiant Chiluba, who dismissed an 11th-hour intervention by South African President Nelson Mandela for a postponement to enable dialogue with Kaunda, told a final campaign rally on Saturday he would ensure there was no violence on Monday.
"We shall make sure there are peaceful elections, our elections will be free and fair," he said. "Those who boycotted and have realised they have boobed will wait until 2001."
Rioting marred the run-up to voting, but many observers predicted apathy and pessimism afterwards rather than civil unrest in copper-rich but desperately debt-ridden Zambia.

But the aid freeze may cripple efforts to service $6.4 billion of debt, bringing new economic hardships for people already reeling from austerity measures and job cuts as Chiluba pursues free-market policies and privatisation.

Political analysts said 53-year-old Chiluba, set to win, would have beaten Kaunda -- and stayed a darling of the West -- even if he had let him stand, but that his manoeuvring may dent support for his Movement for Multiparty Democracy (MMD).
The key election statistic will be not how many votes each of the six contesting parties wins, but how many are cast.
Only half the 4.6 million voters have been registered -- another source of opposition complaint -- and only half of these have received their voting cards.
Kaunda has been campaigning for people to hand in those cards to his United National Independence Party (UNIP). Police say this is illegal and arrested some UNIP officials.
Hoping for a dismally low turnout, Kaunda -- who led Zambia to independence from Britain in 1964 and later ran a one-party state until 1991 -- plans to declare the poll unrepresentative.
He will ask the Chief Justice to run an interim government and call fresh elections, but has little hope of success, diplomats said.
